issues.legal_issue: A trial court’s acquittal should not be reversed in an appeal against acquittal when its view of the evidence is reasonably possible and there is no compelling reason to displace it.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted two accused after finding that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt against them.
The evidence against them established a strained relationship concerning ancestral property, but the recovery of ordinary household items from them was not relied on by the High Court.
The High Court reversed the acquittals and convicted them, although the Supreme Court considered the trial court’s view a possible view of the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in setting aside the acquittals; its convictions were set aside and the appeals of the two accused were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court has power to reappraise the evidence, but the presumption of innocence is reinforced by the acquittal. It must give proper weight and consideration to the trial judge’s assessment of witness credibility, and must not reverse a reasonably possible view merely because it would have taken another view; compelling and weighty reasons are required. No earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment, and no specific statutory provision is identified as the basis for this appellate principle.

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court assessed the evidence and reached a view that was reasonably available on the record.
predicates.motive_is_only_incriminating_circumstanc: The evidence against the accused showed a motive but no other reliable circumstance connecting them to the crime.
predicates.recovery_not_reliable: The alleged recovery from the accused was not relied on as a reliable circumstance connecting them to the crime.
predicates.no_compelling_reason_to_reverse: The appellate court had no compelling and weighty reason to reject the trial court’s assessment.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, a reasonably possible trial-court view based on evidence that shows motive alone, with no reliable recovery or compelling reason to displace that view, means the acquittal should not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence is sustainable only when the proved circumstances form a complete chain pointing to guilt and excluding other reasonable explanations.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness, and the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence.
The evidence established a shared motive relating to the deceased and other accused persons.

Following statements made during the investigation, a dismantled motorcycle wheel and tyre belonging to the deceased were recovered from one accused, and a knife was recovered from another; the recoveries were supported by testimony and seizure records.
Evidence showed that both accused were absent from their usual work soon after the incident.
The trial court convicted the two accused, and the High Court upheld their convictions; the Supreme Court found the circumstances proved beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed their appeal.
issues.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence proved the case beyond reasonable doubt against the two accused, and their convictions were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: For a conviction on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which guilt is inferred must be cogently and firmly established, must unerringly point to guilt, and must form a complete chain that is consistent with guilt and inconsistent with innocence or any other reasonable hypothesis. The assessment depends on the facts of each case. The court applied this principle to convictions for offences under Sections 302 and 201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.
